title: Savitri
hook: a banyan trunk wound with thread: how Savitri is remembered, and how differently she is read

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri on the road behind Death, speaking about the good until he stopped to listen. Your line was Savitri. Did you say something good about a good person, out loud? Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

A banyan tree, its trunk wound round and round with thread. On a festival day called Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, walk around a banyan, and tie thread to it, asking for long lives for their husbands. Vat is the banyan. Savitri is the woman from the forest. The tree itself doesn't come from the epic's telling; it comes from the way the story has been lived since. On our last day with her, the question is how a story becomes a practice, and how one woman can be read in more than one way.
screen: `A BANYAN WOUND WITH THREAD.` → `A FESTIVAL IN HER NAME.` → `ONE WOMAN, MORE THAN ONE READING.`

segments.voice: Start with where the epic puts her. The story sits in the Mahabharata's forest book, and the section that holds it carries a title that can be translated as the greatness of the devoted wife. The sage Markandeya tells it because Yudhishthira has asked him a question: has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? Markandeya's answer is Savitri, and his last word is that Draupadi, like Savitri, will save them all. So the frame is devotion, and some readers keep that frame. They hear in Savitri a wife whose faithfulness is strong enough to stop Death, and the vow with the banyan grows out of that reading. Other readers notice different things in the same lines. Her father sends her out to choose her own husband, and she does. When she's told the man will die, she refuses to choose again. She keeps a hard truth alone for a year. She argues with Death, on the road, as a friend. They hear a woman of fierce will and a sharp mind. And a modern poet, Aurobindo, read her as something else again: the divine word come down to free the soul from death. These readings don't have to cancel each other. Devotion and will can live in one person. What all of them share is a woman who doesn't sit still when the worst news arrives. She acts. Since the story ends here for us, look at how it ended in the epic: Savitri back in the clearing at night, her husband's head in her lap, then picking up his axe and walking him home through the dark.
screen: `THE GREATNESS OF THE DEVOTED WIFE` · `SOME READ DEVOTION STRONG AS DEATH` · `SOME READ A WILL AND A SHARP MIND` · `SHE ACTS WHEN THE WORST NEWS COMES`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie a thread in your mind. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone whose life you'd ask to be long. Hold their face for a moment. Then, slowly, as if you were winding a thread around a tree, go round them in your mind: their morning, their work, their evening, their sleep. One slow circle for each breath, if you like. No need to fix anything. Just keep them company. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Savitri. Told as the greatness of a devoted wife, read by others as a woman of will, and remembered at a banyan wound with thread. Today's word.
Your line: Savitri. Today, do one practical thing for the long life of someone you love: a call, a meal, a reminder about the doctor. Day one thousand three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: On Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, worship at a banyan tree, wind thread around its trunk and hear Savitri's story told, asking for long lives for their husbands; the day and customs differ by region.

notes: Vat Savitri: confirm the description (fasting, circling the banyan, tying thread, for husbands' long lives) and the statement that the banyan is not named in the Mahabharata's telling. Custom and date vary by region (Vat Purnima in some places); howItsDone says so.
'Can be translated as the greatness of the devoted wife' refers to the sub-parva title Pativrata-mahatmya. Confirm wording.
Readings are attributed to some readers and to Aurobindo; no school is named or ranked.
'She keeps a hard truth alone for a year': the epic places the death a year from Narada's words; confirm the phrasing is acceptable.
